name: Technology Strategy and Roadmaps
description: Technology vision, build-buy-partner choices, platform and architecture strategy, roadmapping, technical debt, vendor and migration decisions, innovation balance, outcome measures, AI adoption and M&A due diligence for technology leaders.

cards.subject: Technology vision
says: describes the future state technology should enable for the business
gives teams a long-lived direction to align decisions to
stays stable across several planning cycles
cards.use: need teams to make consistent choices without asking leadership each time
not: lists the projects planned for next quarter

cards.subject: Technology strategy
says: sets the choices and trade-offs that connect technology to business goals
states what the organisation will do and deliberately not do
turns the vision into a coherent set of bets and constraints
cards.use: need to explain why some options are chosen and others are refused
not: is a list of every system the company owns

cards.subject: Strategy kernel
says: combines a diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions
starts by naming the specific challenge that the strategy must overcome
rejects goals-only documents that name no obstacle
cards.use: want a test for whether a strategy document is a real strategy
not: is satisfied by a list of aspirational goals

cards.subject: Wardley mapping
says: places components on a value chain against their evolution stage
shows which parts are genesis, custom, product or commodity
helps decide where to build, buy or outsource by showing maturity
cards.use: need a shared picture of landscape and movement before choosing sourcing
not: scores projects by return on investment

cards.subject: Business-technology alignment
says: links technology investments to named business outcomes
requires the technology leader to understand how the company earns money
is tested by whether business leaders can explain why a system exists
cards.use: notice that funding for technology work is questioned as a cost centre
not: means technology builds whatever the business requests

cards.subject: Capability map
says: lists what the business must be able to do independent of systems or org charts
reveals which capabilities are differentiating and which are commodity
is a stable reference for mapping investments and applications
cards.use: need to see where technology spend sits against business capabilities
not: shows the network topology of the data centre

cards.subject: Strategic differentiator
says: is a capability that customers choose the company for
deserves the best engineers and custom investment
is a candidate for building rather than buying
cards.use: decide which systems merit in-house engineering
not: is any system that is expensive to run

cards.subject: Commodity capability
says: is needed by every company in the sector but does not win customers
is usually better bought or consumed as a service
should receive standard solutions rather than bespoke engineering
cards.use: hear a team propose custom building of payroll or email
not: is always the lowest-risk area to cut

cards.subject: Strategy cascade
says: translates company goals into technology objectives and then team-level bets
lets each level see the goal above it
breaks when teams cannot trace work back to a company goal
cards.use: notice that teams complain that priorities seem arbitrary
not: sends detailed instructions down without any feedback

cards.subject: Build
says: creates the capability in-house with the company's own engineers
gives the most control over behaviour and roadmap
carries ongoing ownership of maintenance, security and staffing
cards.use: judge that the capability is a strategic differentiator
not: has no cost once the first release ships

cards.subject: Buy
says: acquires a ready product or service from a vendor
shortens time to value for non-differentiating capability
trades control and customisation for speed and shared maintenance
cards.use: find that the need is common and a mature product fits most of it
not: removes the need for any internal ownership

cards.subject: Partner
says: shares delivery or capability with another organisation under an agreement
can provide skills or reach the company lacks
creates dependence on the partner's priorities and continuity
cards.use: need a capability fast and want shared risk or channel access
not: gives full control of the partner's roadmap

cards.subject: Total cost of ownership
says: counts run, support, integration, staffing and exit costs as well as purchase price
is the basis for comparing build and buy fairly
grows over years rather than appearing in the first quote
cards.use: notice that build and buy proposals compare only licence against initial development
not: equals the licence fee in the vendor quote

cards.subject: Fit-gap analysis
says: compares the requirements to what a product does out of the box
identifies the gaps that need configuration, custom code or process change
exposes how much customisation a buy decision hides
cards.use: hear a vendor claim their product meets all requirements
not: scores vendors on brand reputation

cards.subject: Core versus context
says: separates activities that differentiate the business from those that merely must work
directs scarce engineering effort to the core
treats context as a candidate for buying or outsourcing
cards.use: notice that engineering time is spent on non-differentiating systems
not: names the parts of the stack with the most users

cards.subject: Hidden cost of customising bought software
says: makes every vendor upgrade a project
erodes the speed advantage that justified buying
turns a product into a bespoke system with none of the control of building
cards.use: inherit a bought package that has been heavily modified over many releases
not: is avoided by customising only through direct database changes

cards.subject: Acqui-hire or acquisition as sourcing
says: buys a team and capability instead of building or licensing them
carries integration and retention risk of key people
needs a plan for what happens to the acquired product
cards.use: need a capability that would take years to hire for
not: transfers knowledge permanently on signing the deal

cards.subject: Open-source adoption
says: avoids licence fees but not support and maintenance cost
requires a plan for security updates and upstream contribution
needs a licence review before use in a product
cards.use: see a team adopt a free library at the heart of a product
not: carries no legal obligations

cards.subject: Platform strategy
says: builds shared capabilities that many product teams reuse
aims to lower the cost and time of delivering each product
succeeds only when product teams choose to use the platform
cards.use: notice that several teams are rebuilding the same plumbing
not: forces every team onto one tool regardless of need

cards.subject: Paved road
says: offers a supported, easy default path for common needs
lets teams leave the path if they accept the extra ownership
reduces cognitive load without banning alternatives
cards.use: want consistency without a central approval board
not: bans every approach other than the default

cards.subject: Golden path template
says: gives a working starter that bakes in standards, security and observability
gets a new service to production in minimal steps
encodes the paved road into reusable scaffolding
cards.use: notice that new services keep being created with inconsistent setup
not: is a document teams read once a year

cards.subject: Platform as a product
says: treats internal teams as customers with needs and feedback
measures adoption and satisfaction rather than mandate
gives the platform team its own roadmap and product owner
cards.use: see teams work around a platform that already exists
not: relies on a mandate to guarantee usage

cards.subject: Conway's law
says: says system structure mirrors the communication structure of the organisation
means team boundaries shape architecture boundaries
implies architecture change may need an organisation change
cards.use: watch an intended architecture keep being undermined by team structure
not: states that systems get faster as teams grow

cards.subject: Inverse Conway manoeuvre
says: designs the team structure to produce the target architecture
aligns teams to desired service boundaries before building them
uses organisation change as a tool for architecture change
cards.use: want a modular architecture but teams are organised by technical layer
not: redraws the architecture diagram and leaves teams alone

cards.subject: Architecture principle
says: is a durable rule guiding design choices across projects
is stated with rationale and implications
helps teams decide consistently without central review
cards.use: notice that architecture review is a bottleneck
not: is a mandatory technology brand list

cards.subject: Enterprise architecture
says: describes how business, data, application and technology layers fit together
supports planning across many teams and systems
fails if it becomes documentation disconnected from delivery
cards.use: need a coherent view across many programmes
not: is the detailed design of a single application

cards.subject: Architecture decision record
says: records a significant decision with its context and consequences
keeps a history of why the system looks as it does
is short and kept with the code or in a shared repository
cards.use: notice that new joiners keep reversing past decisions without knowing the reasons
not: is a ticket describing a bug fix

cards.subject: Reversible versus irreversible decision
says: separates choices that are cheap to undo from those that are costly
allows fast decisions on the reversible kind
calls for more deliberation on the irreversible kind
cards.use: notice that leadership debates every choice with equal ceremony
not: treats all decisions as needing full committee review

cards.subject: Modular monolith
says: keeps one deployable unit with enforced internal module boundaries
avoids distributed-system costs while preserving modularity
can later split into services along the existing boundaries
cards.use: want clean boundaries in a small organisation without microservice overhead
not: is the same as an unstructured big ball of mud

cards.subject: Microservices
says: split a system into independently deployable services
let teams release on their own cadence
add network, data consistency and operational cost
cards.use: notice that many autonomous teams are blocked by a shared deployment
not: always cost less to run than a single deployable

cards.subject: Fitness function
says: is an automated check that an architectural characteristic still holds
turns an architectural intent into a measurable test
guards against gradual drift in a system's structure
cards.use: notice that architectural rules are written down but regularly violated
not: is a quarterly survey of developer happiness

cards.subject: Roadmap
says: communicates planned direction and priorities over time
is a statement of intent rather than a contract
changes as learning and conditions change
cards.use: notice that stakeholders ask where the product or platform is heading
not: promises exact dates for every feature

cards.subject: Outcome-based roadmap
says: frames items as problems to solve or results to achieve
leaves room for teams to choose the solution
avoids committing to a feature list in advance
cards.use: notice that feature-date roadmaps keep breaking
not: lists named features with delivery dates

cards.subject: Now-next-later roadmap
says: groups work by horizon rather than by dated release
signals decreasing certainty for further horizons
avoids false precision about dates
cards.use: notice that leadership wants direction without a dated commitment
not: lists work in strict calendar order

cards.subject: RICE scoring
says: scores reach, impact, confidence and effort to rank items
divides the benefit factors by effort
includes a confidence factor to discount weak estimates
cards.use: need a repeatable way to compare many small initiatives
not: multiplies cost by time to deliver

cards.subject: WSJF
says: ranks work by cost of delay divided by job size
favours small items with high urgency
comes from lean and scaled agile practice
cards.use: notice that delay on some items is much more costly than on others
not: ranks work by the loudest sponsor

cards.subject: Cost of delay
says: quantifies the value lost for each unit of time an item waits
differs between items with the same total value
shows when speed matters more than size of benefit
cards.use: see two projects of equal value compete for the same team
not: is the project budget overrun

cards.subject: MoSCoW
says: sorts requirements into must, should, could and will not
fixes scope by dropping lower categories first when time runs out
forces explicit agreement on what is not included
cards.use: face a fixed deadline with variable scope
not: scores items on a numeric weighted scale

cards.subject: Kano model
says: classifies features as basic, performance or delighters
shows that some features only avoid dissatisfaction
predicts that delighters become expectations over time
cards.use: notice that adding features is no longer raising satisfaction
not: ranks items by engineering effort

cards.subject: Opportunity solution tree
says: maps a desired outcome to opportunities and then candidate solutions
makes the reasoning behind a roadmap item visible
supports comparing several solutions for one opportunity
cards.use: notice that teams jump straight from a goal to a single solution
not: is a hierarchy of the organisation's teams

cards.subject: Capacity planning
says: balances planned work against the actual availability of teams
reserves capacity for incidents, maintenance and debt
exposes that adding items means removing others
cards.use: notice that roadmaps are always overcommitted
not: assumes every team member is fully allocated to features

cards.subject: Dependency mapping
says: reveals which teams and systems must deliver for others to proceed
identifies critical-path cross-team work
helps sequence work to reduce waiting
cards.use: notice that programme delays keep being caused by other teams
not: lists only the external vendors

cards.subject: Three-horizon model
says: labels horizons as core, emerging and future options
expects different return profiles in each horizon
stops the core from starving the new bets
cards.use: notice that leaders need to explain why some bets lack near-term return
not: divides projects into three equal budgets

cards.subject: Technical debt
says: is the future cost created by shortcuts or outdated design choices
slows later change and raises risk until it is repaid
can be a deliberate trade-off when taken knowingly
cards.use: notice that delivery speed has dropped as the code base aged
not: is any bug in the system

cards.subject: Technical debt quadrant
says: classifies debt as deliberate or inadvertent and prudent or reckless
separates conscious trade-offs from ignorance
helps decide whether a fix is policy, training or repayment
cards.use: notice that team disagrees about whether debt was a failure or a choice
not: divides debt by the programming language involved

cards.subject: Debt register
says: lists known debt items with impact, cost and affected area
lets leaders compare debt with feature work
only helps if items are reviewed and prioritised
cards.use: notice that debt is discussed but nobody can quantify it
not: is a log of production incidents

cards.subject: Capacity allocation for debt
says: reserves a standing share of capacity for repayment
prevents debt work from being deferred indefinitely
avoids the need to renegotiate for each item
cards.use: notice that debt is always cut when deadlines tighten
not: schedules a single big clean-up project at year end

cards.subject: Boy scout rule
says: leaves code a little better than it was found
pays small amounts of debt during normal work
does not replace planned work on large structural debt
cards.use: want steady small improvements in areas being changed
not: requires stopping feature work for a rewrite

cards.subject: Interest on debt
says: is the ongoing extra cost of working around the shortcut
is paid every time the affected area changes
makes debt in rarely touched code cheap to leave
cards.use: notice that you must decide which debt to repay first
not: is a fee charged by the cloud provider

cards.subject: Architectural debt
says: lies in structure and boundaries rather than individual lines
is costlier to repay than code-level debt
shows up as changes that touch many modules at once
cards.use: notice that small changes need coordinated edits in many places
not: is fixed by running a code formatter

cards.subject: Deliberate prudent debt
says: is taken knowingly to hit a market window with a plan to repay
is recorded with an owner and trigger for repayment
becomes reckless when the repayment plan is never honoured
cards.use: judge that a launch date matters more than code quality for a defined period
not: is created by developers who do not know better

cards.subject: Technology radar
says: visualises technologies in rings by adoption stance
is a living view reviewed on a regular cadence
shows which technologies are encouraged and which are being phased out
cards.use: want a shared view of which technologies teams should choose
not: is a list of vendor contract end dates

cards.subject: Adopt ring
says: marks technologies that are proven and recommended for general use
signals default choice for new work
comes after evaluation in real use
cards.use: notice that teams need a clear default for a common need
not: marks technologies that are being retired

cards.subject: Trial ring
says: marks technologies worth using on a real project with contained risk
gathers evidence before broad adoption
is for technologies that have shown promise
cards.use: want real-world evidence from a low-risk project
not: marks technologies approved for every team

cards.subject: Assess ring
says: marks technologies worth exploring to understand their potential
does not yet recommend production use
involves reading, prototypes or spikes rather than commitment
cards.use: notice that a new technology looks interesting but is untested here
not: marks technologies recommended as defaults

cards.subject: Hold ring
says: marks technologies that new projects should not start with
applies both to immature and to declining technologies
does not demand immediate removal of existing use
cards.use: want to stop spread of a technology the company is moving away from
not: demands immediate replacement of every instance

cards.subject: Innovation token
says: treats unusual technology choices as a limited budget
encourages boring technology for most of the stack
reserves novelty for where it creates real advantage
cards.use: notice that a team wants a new database, language and framework in one project
not: rewards using the newest option wherever possible

cards.subject: Boring technology
says: favours well understood, proven tools for most needs
has known failure modes and plentiful skills
lowers operational risk and onboarding cost
cards.use: notice that a straightforward need is being solved with an unproven stack
not: avoids all change regardless of benefit

cards.subject: Proof of concept
says: tests technical feasibility of an idea in limited scope
has a defined question and a time limit
is not meant to become the production system
cards.use: need to answer whether an approach can work at all
not: delivers a production-ready release

cards.subject: Pilot
says: tests a solution with real users in a limited setting
measures value and adoption before scaling
needs defined success criteria and exit decision
cards.use: want evidence of real-world value before wider roll-out
not: is an unlimited trial with no end date

cards.subject: Technology lifecycle management
says: tracks each technology from introduction through support to retirement
sets end-of-life dates early enough to plan replacement
prevents unsupported software from silently accumulating
cards.use: notice that nobody knows which components are close to end of support
not: tracks only hardware warranties

cards.subject: Technology rationalisation
says: reduces the number of overlapping tools and platforms
lowers support, licence and skills cost
needs migration funding to deliver the saving
cards.use: notice that the estate has many tools for the same job
not: adds new tools to cover every team's preference

cards.subject: Vendor lock-in
says: makes leaving a supplier costly in money, time or risk
grows with proprietary features and accumulated data
is a trade-off against the speed gained from deep integration
cards.use: notice that leaving a platform would require a rewrite
not: only occurs with open-source software

cards.subject: Exit strategy
says: defines in advance how the company would leave a supplier
covers data export, replacement options and transition time
is part of the decision to adopt, not an afterthought
cards.use: are signing a multi-year contract with a critical supplier
not: is written when the supplier raises its prices

cards.subject: Abstraction layer
says: hides a supplier behind a company-owned interface
lowers switching cost for the abstracted features
adds build cost and may hide useful vendor capabilities
cards.use: want the option to change suppliers for a narrow capability
not: removes lock-in completely at no cost

cards.subject: Multi-cloud
says: spreads workloads over more than one cloud provider
reduces dependence on one provider
adds complexity and reduces use of provider-specific services
cards.use: notice that regulation or risk policy requires provider diversity
not: is cheaper than single-provider by default

cards.subject: Data portability
says: is the ability to extract data in a usable open format
should be tested before the contract ends
directly sets how painful an exit will be
cards.use: are evaluating a software-as-a-service product
not: is guaranteed by the vendor's marketing page

cards.subject: Concentration risk
says: arises when many critical services depend on one supplier
makes a single outage or dispute a company-wide event
is assessed across the whole estate rather than per project
cards.use: notice that many separate teams have independently chosen the same provider
not: is eliminated by negotiating a lower price

cards.subject: Service level agreement
says: commits a supplier to measurable service levels
usually offers credits rather than compensation for loss
covers only what is written in the agreement
cards.use: notice that outages at a supplier hurt the business
not: guarantees zero downtime

cards.subject: Escrow agreement
says: places source code with a neutral third party
releases it if the supplier fails or defaults
protects continuity for a bespoke or critical system
cards.use: notice that a small supplier maintains a critical bespoke system
not: gives the customer ownership of the supplier's product

cards.subject: Vendor scorecard
says: evaluates suppliers against weighted criteria set before demos
reduces the influence of presentations on the decision
includes fit, cost, risk and exit factors
cards.use: notice that selection is driven by whoever gave the best demonstration
not: compares suppliers on logo recognition

cards.subject: Negotiating leverage
says: is strongest before commitment and weakest after deep integration
comes from credible alternatives
declines as switching cost rises
cards.use: notice that renewal pricing from a deeply embedded supplier rises sharply
not: is highest once the product is in production

cards.subject: Strangler fig pattern
says: grows a new system around the old one gradually
routes functions to the new system one slice at a time
retires the old system once nothing depends on it
cards.use: notice that a large legacy system cannot be switched off in one go
not: replaces the whole system in one release

cards.subject: Big-bang migration
says: switches all users to the new system at a single cutover
concentrates risk in one event
needs a tested rollback plan
cards.use: notice that the old and new systems cannot run side by side
not: moves functions across gradually

cards.subject: Parallel run
says: operates old and new systems together on the same inputs
compares outputs to confirm the new system is correct
increases workload and cost during the overlap
cards.use: notice that results of a critical calculation must be proven identical
not: switches users with no overlap period

cards.subject: Rehost
says: moves an application to new infrastructure with minimal change
is the quickest cloud migration approach
captures few of the benefits of cloud-native design
cards.use: notice that a data centre exit deadline is close
not: rewrites the application for cloud services

cards.subject: Replatform
says: moves an application with modest changes to use managed services
keeps the core architecture
balances effort against some cloud benefit
cards.use: want managed database benefits without a rewrite
not: rebuilds the application from scratch

cards.subject: Refactor for the cloud
says: redesigns an application to use cloud-native capabilities
has the highest effort of the migration approaches
delivers the most elasticity and operational benefit
cards.use: notice that an application must scale far beyond its current design
not: moves virtual machines unchanged

cards.subject: Retire
says: switches off applications that are no longer needed
avoids spending migration effort on unused systems
often reveals more candidates than expected in an application review
cards.use: notice that portfolio assessment finds applications with almost no users
not: moves the application to the cloud first

cards.subject: Retain
says: leaves an application where it is for now
is a valid outcome of a portfolio assessment
applies when migration cost exceeds benefit or constraints block a move
cards.use: notice that an application has regulatory or technical constraints
not: means the application is forgotten

cards.subject: Migration wave planning
says: groups applications into ordered batches by dependency and risk
starts with simpler, lower-risk applications to build experience
sequences tightly coupled systems to move together
cards.use: notice that hundreds of applications must be migrated
not: migrates the most critical system first for the signal

cards.subject: Anti-corruption layer
says: translates between a legacy model and a new model
stops legacy concepts from leaking into the new design
is dropped when the legacy system is retired
cards.use: notice that a new system must integrate with a legacy system whose model is poor
not: exposes the legacy data model directly to new code

cards.subject: Data migration risk
says: is a leading cause of failed or delayed cutovers
needs reconciliation checks between source and target
is reduced by rehearsing the migration repeatedly
cards.use: notice that a cutover depends on moving years of data
not: is handled once on the night of cutover

cards.subject: Run-the-business spend
says: covers keeping existing services reliable and supported
is the base load of the technology budget
tends to grow if debt and complexity are not managed
cards.use: notice that most of the budget is consumed by keeping systems alive
not: is investment in new products

cards.subject: Change-the-business spend
says: funds new capabilities and transformation
competes with run costs for the same budget
includes transformation programmes and new product investment
cards.use: notice that leadership asks how much goes to new capability
not: pays for operating existing systems

cards.subject: Ambidextrous organisation
says: exploits existing business while exploring new opportunities
gives exploration its own metrics and protection
avoids judging new bets by the standards of the core
cards.use: notice that innovation projects keep dying in the core process
not: applies identical governance to every initiative

cards.subject: Innovation portfolio
says: spreads investment across many bets of different risk
expects some bets to fail
stops bets early on evidence rather than sunk cost
cards.use: notice that a single large innovation project holds all the budget
not: funds only the most likely winner

cards.subject: Stage-gate funding
says: releases funding in steps as evidence is gathered
limits loss on bets that do not work
needs gate criteria set in advance
cards.use: notice that large bets are approved on a plan alone
not: funds the full cost up front

cards.subject: Lighthouse project
says: demonstrates a new way of working or technology on a visible project
builds credibility and learning for wider adoption
should be representative enough to teach lessons that transfer
cards.use: need to show a new approach works before scaling
not: is a secret side project

cards.subject: OKR
says: pairs an objective with measurable key results
sets ambitious goals reviewed on a short cycle
measures outcomes more than activity
cards.use: want goals that teams can track and align to
not: is a list of tasks with owners

cards.subject: KPI
says: tracks the ongoing health of a business or system area
is monitored continuously rather than set per cycle
signals when something has moved away from normal
cards.use: need to watch steady-state performance
not: is a time-boxed stretch goal

cards.subject: Output versus outcome
says: separates what was delivered from the change it caused
shows that shipping features is not the same as creating value
makes outcome the primary measure of success
cards.use: notice that a team reports many releases but no business change
not: treats number of releases as proof of value

cards.subject: Key result
says: states a measurable result that shows the objective is met
has a baseline and a target
is not a task or deliverable
cards.use: notice that an objective needs evidence of progress
not: lists activities to be completed

cards.subject: Leading indicator
says: moves before the outcome it predicts
lets teams act early
must be shown to correlate with the result
cards.use: notice that results lag so far behind that teams cannot steer
not: reports final results after the period ends

cards.subject: Lagging indicator
says: reports results after the fact
confirms whether an outcome was achieved
is too late to steer in-period work alone
cards.use: need confirmation that goals were reached
not: predicts future results

cards.subject: DORA metrics
says: measure software delivery throughput and stability
include deployment frequency and change failure rate
are used to track delivery capability rather than individual performance
cards.use: want evidence of delivery performance beyond opinion
not: rank individual developers

cards.subject: SPACE framework
says: considers satisfaction, performance, activity, communication and efficiency
warns against measuring developer productivity with one metric
combines several dimensions at different levels
cards.use: notice that a leader asks for a single productivity number
not: recommends counting lines of code

cards.subject: Goodhart's law
says: says a measure ceases to be useful once it becomes a target
explains gaming of metrics
argues for pairing metrics so that gaming one shows up in another
cards.use: notice that a metric improved but the underlying goal did not
not: says targets always improve performance

cards.subject: North star metric
says: is a single measure that best captures the value delivered to customers
aligns teams around one customer-centred outcome
is supported by input metrics that teams can influence
cards.use: notice that teams optimise local numbers that do not add up
not: is a revenue target set by finance

cards.subject: Benefits realisation
says: checks after delivery whether the expected benefits materialised
assigns an owner to each benefit
feeds learning into later investment decisions
cards.use: notice that projects are closed at go-live with no follow-up on value
not: ends at project closure

cards.subject: AI use-case prioritisation
says: scores candidate uses by value, feasibility, data readiness and risk
starts with problems and not with the technology
avoids launching many disconnected experiments
cards.use: notice that many teams propose AI ideas at once
not: picks the use case with the most impressive demonstration

cards.subject: Data readiness
says: determines whether an AI use case can work at all
covers availability, quality, access rights and lineage
is often the real constraint rather than model choice
cards.use: notice that a promising use case depends on messy or siloed data
not: is solved by choosing a stronger model

cards.subject: AI governance
says: sets policies for approved uses, data handling, review and accountability
assigns named owners for AI systems
scales oversight with the risk of each use
cards.use: notice that staff are using unapproved AI tools with company data
not: bans all AI use across the company

cards.subject: Human in the loop
says: keeps a person reviewing or approving AI output before consequences
is applied more strictly to high-impact decisions
needs reviewers with time and ability to challenge the output
cards.use: notice that AI output could affect customers or legal obligations
not: means the model needs no oversight once tested

cards.subject: Model risk management
says: covers validation, monitoring and limits for models in use
tracks drift and performance after deployment
extends to third-party models the company does not control
cards.use: notice that a model in production has not been reviewed since launch
not: ends once the model passes launch tests

cards.subject: AI build versus buy
says: weighs differentiating data and workflow against using vendor models and tools
often combines bought models with company data and workflow
depends on whether the AI capability itself is the differentiator
cards.use: are deciding whether to train a custom model
not: always favours training a proprietary model

cards.subject: Evaluation harness
says: measures AI system quality on a representative test set
lets changes of model or prompt be compared objectively
is built before scaling a use case
cards.use: notice that changing the model breaks things nobody notices
not: is replaced by trying a few prompts by hand

cards.subject: Shadow AI
says: is the use of unsanctioned AI tools by staff
creates data leakage and compliance risk
is reduced by offering approved alternatives as well as rules
cards.use: notice that employees paste customer data into public chat tools
not: is AI that runs only at night

cards.subject: AI total cost
says: includes usage fees, integration, evaluation, monitoring and change effort
can scale with volume in a way fixed licences do not
should be modelled at production volume not pilot volume
cards.use: notice that a pilot looked cheap but production usage is large
not: is the licence price of the model

cards.subject: Pilot-to-production gap
says: describes the many AI pilots that never reach daily use
stems from missing integration, data, ownership and change management
is narrowed by planning production needs at the start
cards.use: notice that a demo impressed leadership six months ago and nothing shipped
not: is caused only by weak models

cards.subject: AI augmentation versus automation
says: augmentation supports people while automation replaces a task
augmentation is lower risk when errors are costly
the choice depends on error tolerance and the cost of review
cards.use: are deciding how much autonomy to give an AI workflow
not: treats both as the same level of risk

cards.subject: Technical due diligence
says: assesses the technology, team and risks of an acquisition target
tests claims made in the sales process
feeds valuation and integration planning
cards.use: notice that the company is about to acquire another business
not: is the financial audit of the target

cards.subject: Code and architecture review
says: inspects structure, quality, test coverage and maintainability
indicates how costly the system will be to extend
is sampled and focused when the code base is large
cards.use: need to know how healthy the target's product is
not: counts developers to estimate quality

cards.subject: Open-source licence audit
says: scans the code base for third-party and copyleft licences
finds obligations that could affect ownership or distribution
is a standard check before an acquisition
cards.use: notice that the target ships software built from many libraries
not: only checks the target's own source files

cards.subject: Security and compliance assessment
says: reviews breaches, controls, certifications and vulnerabilities
identifies liabilities the buyer would inherit
checks data handling against regulation
cards.use: notice that the target holds customer personal data
not: accepts a certificate as complete proof of security

cards.subject: Key-person dependency
says: is the risk that critical knowledge sits with a few individuals
needs retention and knowledge-transfer plans
is assessed through interviews as well as documents
cards.use: notice that one engineer built and understands the core platform
not: is reduced by buying out the founders

cards.subject: Scalability and infrastructure review
says: tests whether systems can handle projected growth
examines cloud use, resilience and cost per customer
reveals hidden spending needed after the deal
cards.use: notice that the deal case assumes much higher volumes
not: accepts the target's capacity claims on trust

cards.subject: Integration plan
says: sets how systems, teams and data will combine after the deal
decides what to merge, keep separate or retire
starts during diligence rather than after close
cards.use: notice that two overlapping platforms will exist after acquisition
not: is written after the deal has closed

cards.subject: Synergy validation
says: tests whether the promised technology savings are achievable
challenges assumptions behind cost and revenue synergies
often finds integration costs higher than first expected
cards.use: notice that the deal rationale relies on consolidating platforms
not: accepts deal-model synergies as given

cards.subject: Red flag finding
says: is an issue that could change price, structure or the decision itself
is escalated to deal leaders promptly
is separated from minor issues in the report
cards.use: notice that diligence uncovers unlicensed code in the core product
not: is listed with the other findings in an appendix

cards.subject: Technology debt valuation
says: estimates the cost of bringing the target's systems to an acceptable standard
may be used to adjust price or agree remediation commitments
is a view on future spend not a historical figure
cards.use: notice that the target has outdated systems and the price assumes none
not: is ignored because the price is already agreed

cards.subject: Technology operating model
says: describes how technology is organised, funded, governed and delivered
covers structure, process, funding and sourcing together
needs to change when the strategy changes
cards.use: notice that strategy has shifted and delivery still follows the old structure
not: is the list of systems in the estate

cards.subject: Project-to-product shift
says: funds enduring teams around products instead of time-boxed projects
keeps ownership after release
measures outcomes over the life of the product
cards.use: notice that systems degrade after each project team disbands
not: funds each initiative as a separate temporary project

cards.subject: Centralised technology organisation
says: keeps all technology staff in a central department
gives consistent standards and efficient shared skills
can be slow to respond to individual business units
cards.use: need consistency and shared specialist skills
not: places engineers inside each business team

cards.subject: Embedded technology teams
says: place engineers inside business or product teams
give close alignment and fast response
risk inconsistent standards and duplicated work
cards.use: notice that business units need speed and context
not: pool all engineers in one central group

cards.subject: Federated model
says: combines a central core with technology teams in business units
sets common standards while allowing local ownership
needs clear rules on which decisions are central
cards.use: want both consistency and local responsiveness
not: removes the need for any central governance

cards.subject: Team Topologies
says: defines stream-aligned, platform, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams
limits cognitive load on each team
uses defined interaction modes between teams
cards.use: notice that team boundaries and interactions are unclear
not: prescribes one standard team size for all cases

cards.subject: Centre of excellence
says: gathers specialists to set practice and support other teams
speeds up adoption of a new capability
risks becoming a bottleneck if it does the work instead of enabling
cards.use: notice that a new capability such as data engineering needs to spread
not: owns all delivery of the capability

cards.subject: Insourcing versus outsourcing
says: weighs control and knowledge retention against flexibility and cost
depends on whether the capability is core
needs governance and exit planning when outsourced
cards.use: are deciding who should run an operational function
not: is settled by the lowest hourly rate

cards.subject: Build-operate-transfer
says: has a partner build and run a capability then hand it to the company
moves ownership once the company is ready
needs agreed transfer terms and knowledge handover
cards.use: want a new captive capability without building it from nothing
not: keeps the partner as permanent operator

cards.subject: Skills strategy
says: plans which skills to hire, train or buy against future needs
links workforce plans to the technology roadmap
accepts that hiring alone cannot close every gap
cards.use: notice that the roadmap needs skills the company does not have
not: assumes the market will supply any skill on demand

cards.subject: Governance model
says: defines who decides what in technology investment and standards
should be light for low-risk and strict for high-risk decisions
becomes a bottleneck if every decision needs central approval
cards.use: notice that decision rights are unclear across teams
not: requires committee approval for every change

cards.subject: Resume-driven development
says: selects technology to build the team's CVs rather than to fit the need
adds unneeded complexity and skills risk
is countered by clear selection criteria and decision records
cards.use: notice that a team picks a fashionable stack for a simple problem
not: describes choosing proven tools after a fair comparison

cards.subject: Not-invented-here syndrome
says: rejects external solutions simply because they are not built in-house
wastes effort on non-differentiating work
is balanced by core-versus-context thinking
cards.use: notice that a team builds its own version of a commodity tool
not: describes preferring external products to bespoke code

cards.subject: Shiny object syndrome
says: chases new technologies before value is shown
fragments the stack and splits attention
is limited by an adoption process with evidence gates
cards.use: notice that strategy changes direction whenever a new trend appears
not: describes keeping to proven technology

cards.subject: Big-bang rewrite
says: replaces a working system in one large effort
delays value until the end and often underestimates hidden behaviour
is usually safer replaced by incremental modernisation
cards.use: notice that leadership proposes rewriting the platform from scratch
not: is a low-risk way to remove debt

cards.subject: Ivory-tower architecture
says: produces designs without involvement from the delivering teams
is ignored or worked around in practice
is avoided by shared ownership of decisions
cards.use: notice that architects publish standards that teams do not follow
not: describes architects working within delivery teams

cards.subject: Strategy as a list of projects
says: names initiatives without stating choices or reasons
cannot guide trade-offs
is not a strategy under the kernel test
cards.use: notice that the strategy document is a long plan of programmes
not: makes explicit what the company will not do

cards.subject: Roadmap as a commitment trap
says: treats dates on a roadmap as promises
leads to teams shipping features to meet dates regardless of value
is avoided by communicating confidence and horizons
cards.use: notice that stakeholders hold teams to dated features set a year earlier
not: treats the roadmap as a statement of intent

cards.subject: Sunk cost fallacy
says: continues a failing initiative because of past spend
ignores that past cost cannot be recovered
is countered by deciding on future costs and benefits
cards.use: notice that a programme is far behind but leadership says too much is already spent
not: describes stopping a project when evidence turns against it

qa.q: What is the main purpose of a technology roadmap?
qa.right: To communicate planned direction and priorities over time
wrong: To record every defect found in the last release
To commit to exact delivery dates for each feature
To list the licences the company holds
qa.why: A roadmap communicates intent and direction; it is not a contract or an inventory.

qa.q: Which question best separates a strategy from a list of goals?
qa.right: What obstacle does it address and what will we do about it?
wrong: How many goals does it contain?
qa.why: A real strategy diagnoses a challenge and sets a policy and actions.

qa.q: For which capability is building in-house most justified?
qa.right: One that customers choose the company for
qa.why: Differentiating capability deserves custom investment; commodity capability is usually bought.

qa.q: Which ring on a technology radar tells teams not to start new work with a technology?
qa.right: Hold
qa.why: Hold means do not start new projects with it; existing use is not necessarily removed at once.

qa.q: Which factors does RICE scoring combine?
qa.right: Reach, impact, confidence and effort
qa.why: RICE is reach times impact times confidence divided by effort.

qa.q: A company compares build against buy by looking only at the first-year licence and initial development cost. What is missing?
qa.right: Run, support, integration, staffing and exit costs over several years
wrong: The number of features in the demo
qa.why: Total cost of ownership covers the full life, not just the first-year price.

qa.q: What does the inverse Conway manoeuvre do?
qa.right: Shapes team structure to produce the target architecture
wrong: Draws the architecture to match the current org chart
qa.why: Since structure mirrors communication, change the teams to change the system.

qa.q: What is the best description of a paved road in platform strategy?
qa.right: A supported default path teams can leave if they accept extra ownership
wrong: A mandatory standard with no exceptions
qa.why: Paved roads make the right way the easy way without banning alternatives.

qa.q: Which measure group covers deployment frequency and change failure rate?
qa.right: DORA metrics
qa.why: DORA measures software delivery throughput and stability.

qa.q: What does WSJF divide by job size?
qa.right: Cost of delay
qa.why: WSJF ranks by cost of delay over size, favouring short urgent items.

qa.q: Which statement about a key result is correct?
qa.right: It is a measurable result with a baseline and a target
wrong: It is a task assigned to a team
It is the title of the objective
It cannot be changed during the quarter
qa.why: Key results show the objective is met; tasks are not key results.

qa.q: What does Goodhart's law warn about?
qa.right: A measure used as a target stops being a good measure
qa.why: People optimise the number, not what it was meant to represent.

qa.q: Which approach reduces the risk of replacing a large legacy system?
qa.right: Strangler fig: move slices behind a stable interface over time
wrong: Freeze all change for a year and rewrite
Replace everything on one cutover weekend with no rollback
Rewrite the least critical part first and stop there
qa.why: Incremental replacement delivers value earlier and limits the blast radius.

qa.q: Why is data readiness often the real constraint in AI adoption?
qa.right: Without accessible, good-quality, permitted data the use case cannot work, whatever the model
wrong: Data is always more expensive than models
qa.why: The model is rarely the limiting factor; the data usually is.

qa.q: Which migration option moves an application with almost no change?
qa.right: Rehost
qa.why: Rehost, or lift and shift, changes the infrastructure and little else.

qa.q: A pilot of an AI assistant was cheap, but production costs are many times higher. What was most likely missed?
qa.right: Modelling cost at production volume, including integration and monitoring
qa.why: Pilot cost does not scale linearly; usage-based pricing and operations grow with volume.

qa.q: Which risk is specific to heavy customisation of a bought package?
qa.right: Every vendor upgrade becomes a project
wrong: The vendor can no longer be paid
The package stops running on any hardware
qa.why: Customisation erodes the speed benefit of buying.

qa.q: What is the purpose of an architecture decision record?
qa.right: To capture why a significant decision was made and its consequences
qa.why: Context and consequences preserve reasoning for later teams.

qa.q: What distinguishes a proof of concept from a pilot?
qa.right: A proof of concept tests feasibility; a pilot tests value with real users
wrong: A pilot has no time limit
A proof of concept is always in production
qa.why: Feasibility first, then value in real use.

qa.q: Which is run-the-business spend?
qa.right: Keeping existing systems supported and reliable
qa.why: Run spend maintains what exists; change spend creates new capability.

qa.q: What is an advantage of the federated technology model?
qa.right: Common standards with local ownership in business units
wrong: All engineers sit in one department
Each unit picks any tool with no limits
qa.why: Federation combines a central core with local responsiveness.

qa.q: What does the Team Topologies idea of limiting cognitive load imply?
qa.right: Each team should own only as much as it can understand and run effectively
wrong: Teams should be as large as possible
Every team should own the full stack of the company
Platform teams should avoid helping other teams
qa.why: Team scope should fit what the team can hold in its head.

qa.q: What is the purpose of an exit strategy in a vendor decision?
qa.right: To define how the company would leave, including data export and replacement, before committing
wrong: To plan the vendor's own departure
qa.why: Exit planning is done at adoption, when leverage is highest.

qa.q: Which technical due diligence finding most directly affects ownership of the product?
qa.right: Copyleft-licensed code embedded in the core product
qa.why: Licence obligations can affect distribution and ownership, unlike style issues.

qa.q: What does a fitness function do?
qa.right: Automatically tests that an architectural characteristic still holds
wrong: Draws dependency diagrams for the board
qa.why: It turns architectural intent into an automated check.

qa.q: What does an escrow agreement protect?
qa.right: Continuity for a critical system if the supplier fails
qa.why: Source code is released to the customer on defined triggers.

qa.q: What distinguishes a leading from a lagging indicator?
qa.right: A leading indicator moves before the outcome and allows early action
wrong: A leading indicator is always more accurate
A lagging indicator predicts future results
They are both reported after the period
qa.why: Lagging indicators confirm results; leading ones help steer.

qa.q: Which tool shows components by evolution from genesis to commodity?
qa.right: Wardley map
qa.why: Wardley maps position components on a value chain against evolution.

qa.q: Which statement about deliberate prudent technical debt is correct?
qa.right: It is acceptable only with an owner and a plan for repayment
qa.why: The plan and owner are what make it prudent.

qa.q: Why do roadmaps framed as outcomes help?
qa.right: They define the problem and leave teams to choose the solution
wrong: They remove the need for priorities
qa.why: Outcomes allow learning to shape solutions.

qa.q: A CTO sees that three teams have each built their own deployment tooling. Teams say the central platform is hard to use. What should the CTO do first?
qa.right: Treat the platform as a product: find out why teams avoid it and fix those gaps
wrong: Mandate the platform by policy and punish workarounds
Let each team keep its own tooling permanently
Replace the platform team with an external vendor immediately
qa.why: Adoption problems are product problems; mandate hides them.

qa.q: A board member asks the CTO to rewrite the legacy order system from scratch in 18 months because it is slow to change. What is the best response?
qa.right: Propose incremental replacement of slices with value delivered along the way
wrong: Agree and halt all other work on it
Refuse any change to the system
Outsource the rewrite with a fixed price and no gates
qa.why: Incremental modernisation keeps value flowing and exposes hidden behaviour early.

qa.q: A critical SaaS supplier proposes a three-year renewal with a large price rise. Data export is difficult and no alternative has been assessed. What was the earlier mistake?
qa.right: No exit strategy or credible alternative was kept, so negotiating leverage was lost
qa.why: Leverage disappears as switching cost rises; alternatives and portability must be maintained.

qa.q: Teams are asked to deliver every committed roadmap item by date, and quality is dropping. What is the likely cause?
qa.right: The roadmap is being treated as a commitment rather than as intent
qa.why: Date commitments push teams to ship regardless of value and quality.

qa.q: Delivery speed has fallen and engineers blame old code. Leadership wants a figure for the cost. What is the best first step?
qa.right: Build a debt register linking items to the extra cost they add to upcoming work
wrong: Order a code formatter run across the repository
Ask engineers to estimate lines of code
Stop all feature work for a quarter
qa.why: Quantifying interest against planned work enables prioritisation.

qa.q: A company with an acquisition due to close finds the target's core product depends on one engineer who plans to leave. What should the buyer do?
qa.right: Raise it as a red flag and secure retention and knowledge transfer before close
wrong: Ignore it because the code is documented
Wait until after integration to discuss it
qa.why: Key-person dependency can change price and structure.

qa.q: Staff are pasting customer records into public AI chat tools. What is the best response?
qa.right: Provide approved tools and clear policy with monitoring, rather than relying on a ban alone
wrong: Ban all AI and stop there
Move all staff to a single public tool
qa.why: Bans without alternatives drive more shadow use.

qa.q: A promising AI pilot impressed executives, yet nothing has reached daily use after six months. What is the most probable gap?
qa.right: No plan for integration, data, ownership and change management for production
wrong: The pilot used too few prompts
qa.why: Pilots fail to scale mainly for operational reasons.

qa.q: A team wants a new language, database and message broker for a simple internal tool. How should the CTO respond?
qa.right: Ask which choice is needed for advantage and steer the rest to proven technology
wrong: Approve all three because the team is motivated
Make the team write a rewrite proposal for existing systems
qa.why: Innovation tokens should be spent where novelty creates real advantage.

qa.q: Two equally valuable projects compete for one team. One loses a large revenue stream for each month of delay; the other does not. How do you decide?
qa.right: Do the one with the higher cost of delay first
wrong: Do the one with more sponsors
qa.why: Cost of delay shows the price of waiting.

qa.q: A company wants a modular architecture but its teams are organised by layer: front end, back end, database. What is the most effective step?
qa.right: Reorganise into stream-aligned teams owning end-to-end slices
wrong: Document the target architecture more thoroughly
qa.why: Structure mirrors communication, so team design must change.

qa.q: After a merger, two platforms provide the same service. The deal model assumes savings by next year. What should the CTO check first?
qa.right: Whether the integration plan and migration cost really support the synergy timing
wrong: Which platform has the nicer interface
qa.why: Synergy claims often ignore migration cost and sequencing.

qa.q: A team proposes to build its own email and calendar system for security reasons. What principle applies?
qa.right: Commodity capabilities should be bought unless a specific requirement cannot be met
wrong: Email is a strategic differentiator for all firms
qa.why: Core versus context directs effort away from commodity.

qa.q: A programme is behind and over budget, but leaders say stopping would waste money already spent. What is the best decision basis?
qa.right: Expected future cost and benefit from this point
qa.why: Past spend is sunk and should not drive the decision.

qa.q: Product teams report metrics going up, but customers see no improvement. What should the CTO suspect?
qa.right: Metrics are being gamed or measure outputs instead of outcomes
qa.why: Goodhart's law and output focus are common causes.

qa.q: A regulated firm must show it can survive the failure of its main cloud provider. What is a fitting response?
qa.right: Assess concentration risk and plan an exit or fallback for critical services
wrong: Buy more services from that provider
qa.why: Concentration risk requires tested exit and fallback.

qa.q: A Hackathon produced many prototypes, but none have gone further. What would help most?
qa.right: A defined path and funding route for promising ideas
qa.why: Ideas need somewhere to go.

qa.q: The estate has five overlapping monitoring tools and rising support cost. What is the best approach?
qa.right: Rationalise to a few tools, funding the migration
wrong: Add a sixth tool to unify them
qa.why: Savings need migration funding.

qa.q: A migration of 400 applications is planned. Which sequencing is best?
qa.right: Start with simple, low-risk applications and move tightly coupled ones together in waves
wrong: Migrate the most critical systems first
Migrate one team at a time regardless of dependencies
qa.why: Early waves build experience; dependencies determine groupings.

qa.q: A team wants to build a custom model for a task that a bought model with company data could handle. What should the CTO ask?
qa.right: Is the model itself a differentiator or is the data and workflow?
wrong: Which model has the most parameters?
Can we name it after the company?
qa.why: Often differentiation lies in data and workflow.

qa.q: A new CTO finds that many decisions are escalated to a central committee, slowing delivery. What is an appropriate change?
qa.right: Separate reversible decisions for teams to take from irreversible ones for review
qa.why: Reversibility determines the right level of ceremony.

qa.q: A strategy document lists 40 projects but no trade-offs or reasons. What is wrong with it?
qa.right: It lacks a diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions
qa.why: This is a list of projects, not a strategy.

qa.q: A vendor claims its product meets every requirement. How can the CTO test it?
qa.right: Run a fit-gap analysis against requirements with a scripted demonstration
wrong: Wait for references from the vendor only
qa.why: Fit-gap exposes hidden customisation.

qa.q: A platform team measures success by the number of services on the platform, but satisfaction is low. What is wrong?
qa.right: The measure rewards mandate and adoption count, not value to users
wrong: The platform has too few features
qa.why: Platform success is value delivered to internal customers.

qa.q: Engineers spend most of their time on maintenance. Which measure will best track the problem?
qa.right: The keeping-the-lights-on ratio over time
qa.why: It shows how much capacity remains for change.

qa.q: A company is deciding whether to outsource its service desk. Which factor should come first?
qa.right: Whether the function is core to its advantage and what exit would look like
qa.why: Sourcing follows capability importance, plus exit planning.

qa.q: A new technology looks promising but untested in the company. Which radar ring is right?
qa.right: Assess
qa.why: Assess is for exploring before committing to use.

qa.q: Which roadmap format avoids false precision about dates?
qa.right: Now-next-later
qa.why: It groups by horizon.

qa.q: A company runs two systems in parallel for months during migration and the overlap is expensive. When is this still justified?
qa.right: When output correctness of a critical function must be proven before cutover
qa.why: Parallel runs trade cost for proof.
